5.7.5 Interest Coverage Ratio
It is a ratio which deals with the servicing of interest on loan. It is a measure of
security of interest payable on long-term debts. It expresses the relationship
between profits available for payment of interest and the amount of interest
payable. It is calculated as follows:
Interest Coverage Ratio = Net Profit before Interest and Tax
Interest on long-term debts
Significance: It reveals the number of times interest on long-term debts is covered
by the profits available for interest. A higher ratio ensures safety of interest on
debts.
Illustration 11
From the following details, calculate interest coverage

ratio:
Net Profit after tax Rs. 60,000; 15% Long-term debt 10,00,000; and Tax rate
40%.
Solution:
Net Profit after Tax = Rs. 60,000
Tax Rate = 40%
Net Profit before tax = Net profit after tax × 100/(100 – Tax rate)
= Rs. 60,000 × 100/(100 – 40)
= Rs. 1,00,000
Interest on Long-term Debt = 15% of Rs. 10,00,000 = Rs. 1,50,000
Net profit before interest and tax = Net profit before tax + Interest
= Rs. 1,00,000 + Rs. 1,50,000 = Rs. 2,50,000
Interest Coverage Ratio = Net Profit before Interest and
Tax/Interest on long-term debt
= Rs. 2,50,000/Rs. 1,50,000
= 1.67 times.

supporting_spans.quote:
5.7.5 Interest Coverage Ratio
It is a ratio which deals with the servicing of interest on loan. It is a measure of
security of interest payable on long-term debts. It expresses the relationship
between profits available for payment of interest and the amount of interest
payable. It is calculated as follows:
Interest Coverage Ratio = Net Profit before Interest and Tax
Interest on long-term debts
Significance: It reveals the number of times interest on long-term debts is covered
by the profits available for interest. A higher ratio ensures safety of interest on
debts.
Illustration 11
From the following details, calculate interest coverage

ratio:
Net Profit after tax Rs. 60,000; 15% Long-term debt 10,00,000; and Tax rate
40%.
Solution:
Net Profit after Tax = Rs. 60,000
Tax Rate = 40%
Net Profit before tax = Net profit after tax × 100/(100 – Tax rate)
= Rs. 60,000 × 100/(100 – 40)
= Rs. 1,00,000
Interest on Long-term Debt = 15% of Rs. 10,00,000 = Rs. 1,50,000
Net profit before interest and tax = Net profit before tax + Interest
= Rs. 1,00,000 + Rs. 1,50,000 = Rs. 2,50,000
Interest Coverage Ratio = Net Profit before Interest and
Tax/Interest on long-term debt
= Rs. 2,50,000/Rs. 1,50,000
= 1.67 times.

supporting_spans.quote: 6.1 THE BALANCE OF PAYMENTS The balance of payments (BoP) record the transactions in goods, services and assets between residents of a country with the rest of the world for a specified time period typically a year. There are two main accounts in the BoP — the current account and the capital account1. 6.1.1 Current Account Current Account is the record of trade in goods and services and transfer payments. Figure 6.1 illustrates the components of Current Account. Trade in goods includes exports and imports of goods. Trade in services includes factor income and non-factor income transactions. Transfer payments are the receipts which the

of imports of invisibles of a country in a given period of time. Invisibles include services, transfers and flows of income that take place between different countries. Services trade includes both factor and non-factor income. Factor income includes net international earnings on factors of production (like labour, land and capital). Non-factor income is net sale of service products like shipping, banking, tourism, software services, etc. 6.1.2 Capital Account Capital Account records all international transactions of assets. An asset is any one of the forms in which wealth can be held, for example: money, stocks, bonds, Government debt, etc.

Purchase of assets is a debit item on the capital account. If an Indian buys a UK Car Company, it enters capital account transactions as a debit item (as foreign exchange is flowing out of India). On the other hand, sale of assets like sale of share of an Indian company to a Chinese customer is a credit item on the capital account. Fig. 6.2 classifies the items which are a part of capital account transactions. These items are Foreign Direct Investments (FDIs), Foreign Institutional Investments (FIIs), external borrowings and assistance.

defects: unsupported_fact_or_explanation: The excerpts do not establish the decisive credit-side treatment of service exports or inward FDI, so the key cannot be verified from the supplied sources.

reasons: Statement 1 is true: The current account records trade in goods and services; export of services (such as financial or banking services) brings foreign exchange into the domestic economy and is credited to the current account.

Statement 2 is true: The capital account records international transactions in assets; Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) into India represents an inflow of foreign exchange (sale of domestic equity/assets to non-residents), which is recorded on the credit side of the capital account.
Since both statements are true, Option C is the correct answer.

question.body: A case illustrates increasing participation of women in the workforce through Sapna, a woman who recently joined a company and uses accounting software at work. Which two business-environment dimensions are highlighted?
question.explanation: Increasing participation of women in the workforce is a social-environment element in NCERT, and using accounting software is a technological-environment element. The case supplies no government attitude (political), no economic variable and no legislation (legal), so the pairs containing political, economic or legal are not supported.

learning_objective.why_answer_requires_it: The student must link each detail in the case to a dimension of the business environment.

reasons: E1.1 identifies shifts in women's presence in the workforce as a social factor. Accounting software relates to technological methods and techniques of operating a business (E2.1; E4.1). Thus the dimensions are social and technological: option A.

question.subject: english
question.body: How can the solutions suggested in paragraph 5 best be described?
question.explanation: Paragraph 5 proposes concrete measures: traceable ownership so that dumping can be fined, refundable deposits for returning or recycling nets, sonar reflectors to locate nets, and working with small-scale fisheries on more sustainable gear. These are measures that can be carried out successfully, which is what practical means. Presentable concerns looking suitable or good enough, popular means liked by many people and prejudiced means showing an unreasonable dislike; the paragraph supports none of these.
question.passage_text:
(1) A ghost net is a fishing net lost or abandoned in the ocean. Although fishers no longer use it, it keeps working, trapping marine life. Abandoned fishing gear creates a wider problem known as ghost fishing.

(2) Ghost nets entangle turtles, dolphins, birds, sharks, seals and fish. They restrict movement, cause injuries and prevent mammals and birds from reaching air. Hundreds of animals can be caught in one net, making the threat monumental. Nets also break corals, exposing them to disease and blocking needed sunlight.

(3) Most modern nets contain nylon or other plastics that can last for centuries. Ghost nets contribute to the Great Pacific Garbage Patch. When they break down, they become smaller plastic pieces rather than disappearing. Animals mistake these microplastics for food. question.subject: english
question.body: Select the option that conveys the opposite of “negligible”, using a word from paragraph 2.
question.explanation: Negligible means small and not important. Paragraph 2 calls the threat monumental, meaning very big or very great, which is the opposite of small and not important. Unimpressive means not making you feel admiration or respect, exposing means putting someone at risk, and threat means the possibility that something unwanted will happen; none of these is opposite in size or importance.
question.passage_text:
(1) A ghost net is a fishing net lost or abandoned in the ocean. Although fishers no longer use it, it keeps working, trapping marine life. Abandoned fishing gear creates a wider problem known as ghost fishing.

(2) Ghost nets entangle turtles, dolphins, birds, sharks, seals and fish. They restrict movement, cause injuries and prevent mammals and birds from reaching air. Hundreds of animals can be caught in one net, making the threat monumental. Nets also break corals, exposing them to disease and blocking needed sunlight.

(3) Most modern nets contain nylon or other plastics that can last for centuries. Ghost nets contribute to the Great Pacific Garbage Patch. When they break down, they become smaller plastic pieces rather than disappearing. Animals mistake these microplastics for food. Eating them can harm internal organs, prevent further feeding and expose animals to toxic chemicals.

(4) Removing ghost nets requires commitment, cooperation and innovation. Conservation groups work with local fishers and governments to locate abandoned gear and remove it from the sea.

(5) Preventing abandonment also matters. Conservation organisations suggest traceable ownership so people dumping nets can be fined, and refundable deposits to encourage returning or recycling nets. Sonar reflectors can help locate lost nets. Working with small-scale fisheries can develop more sustainable gear and practices. Tackling the problem from several sides, with conservation partners, fishers and supporters, can help protect the oceans.

question.subject: economics
question.body: Statement 1: Net investment is a stock concept. Statement 2: Capital is a flow concept. Choose the correct option.

options.text: Statement 1 is true and Statement 2 is false.
Statement 1 is false and Statement 2 is true.

question.explanation: NCERT defines a stock at a particular point of time, and the capital goods in an economy are a stock. Changes in stock over a period are flows, and net investment (gross investment minus depreciation) is the new addition to the capital stock over a period, so it is a flow. Statement 1 calls net investment a stock and Statement 2 calls capital a flow, so both reverse the classification and both are false.

question.subject: business_studies
question.body: An automobile company divides work into production, purchase, marketing, accounts and personnel. Which of the following is a disadvantage of this organisation structure?

options.text: It may lead to an increase in cost.
Managers may gain power, assert independence and ignore organisational interests.
It ensures that different functions get due attention.
Heads do not get training for top management positions.

question.explanation: Dividing work into production, purchase, marketing, accounts and personnel departments forms a functional structure. NCERT lists among its disadvantages that functional heads do not get training for top management positions because they cannot gather experience in diverse areas. Ensuring that different functions get due attention is an advantage of this structure.

learning_objective.why_answer_requires_it: The student must recognise the structure from its departments and recall its listed disadvantages.

question.body: Changes in the business environment occur so frequently that predicting future developments becomes difficult. Which characteristic is most directly highlighted?
question.explanation: NCERT describes uncertainty as the feature that the business environment is very difficult to predict, especially when changes take place too frequently. Complexity concerns many interrelated forces that are hard to comprehend at once, inter-relatedness concerns elements that affect each other, and relativity concerns differences from country to country and region to region.

question.subject: economics
question.body: Consider the NCERT two-sector income–expenditure model, with autonomous investment and a constant marginal propensity to consume strictly between 0 and 1. Statement 1: The consumption curve is an upward-sloping straight line because consumption rises with income at a constant rate. Statement 2: The aggregate-demand curve and consumption curve are parallel. Choose the correct option.

options.text: Statement 1 is true and Statement 2 is false.
Statement 1 is false and Statement 2 is true.

question.explanation: With a constant marginal propensity to consume c, consumption = autonomous consumption + cY rises with income at a constant rate, so it is an upward-sloping straight line and Statement 1 is true. In the two-sector model investment is autonomous, and aggregate demand is obtained by vertically adding that constant investment to consumption, so the aggregate demand function has the same slope c as the consumption function and the two are parallel; Statement 2 is true as well.

learning_objective.syllabus_unit: Course II Unit III: Determination of Income and Employment
learning_objective.objective: Compare the consumption function and the aggregate demand function in the two-sector model.
learning_objective.why_answer_requires_it: The student must connect a constant marginal propensity to consume with the slopes of both functions.

learning_objective.objective: Compare the consumption function and the aggregate demand function in the two-sector model.
learning_objective.why_answer_requires_it: The student must connect a constant marginal propensity to consume with the slopes of both functions.

reasons: With a constant MPC c strictly between 0 and 1, consumption is C = C̄ + cY, so its slope is positive and it is an upward-sloping straight line (E1.1, E1.2).

In the two-sector model, aggregate demand is C + I. Autonomous investment is constant with respect to income, so adding it shifts the consumption curve without changing its slope; the curves are parallel (E2.1, E3.1). Both statements are true: C.
The strict MPC bounds exclude c = 0, which would make consumption horizontal; at c = 1 the curves would still be upward-sloping and parallel, but that boundary is also excluded.
source_support.syllabus_topic: Consumption function and aggregate demand in the two-sector income–expenditure model; their slopes and parallelism.

answer_conditions.condition: The model is two-sector, with consumption and investment as the components of aggregate demand.
Investment is autonomous and therefore does not vary with income.
The marginal propensity to consume is constant and strictly between 0 and 1.

option_challenges.strongest_reading: If investment varied with income, aggregate demand could have a different slope from consumption even when consumption rose linearly.
At MPC = 0, consumption would be horizontal while adding autonomous investment would leave aggregate demand parallel to it.
With a zero or nonconstant MPC, consumption need not be upward linear; income-dependent investment could also make aggregate demand nonparallel.

question.subject: accountancy
question.body: For one financial year, a company has net profit after tax of ₹12,00,000, 10% debentures of ₹1,00,00,000, and a tax rate of 40%. The debentures were outstanding throughout the year and are its only interest-bearing debt. Calculate its interest coverage ratio.
question.explanation: Interest coverage ratio = profit before interest and tax divided by interest on long-term debt. Interest = 10% of ₹1,00,00,000 = ₹10,00,000. Profit before tax = ₹12,00,000 × 100/(100 − 40) = ₹20,00,000. Profit before interest and tax = ₹20,00,000 + ₹10,00,000 = ₹30,00,000. Ratio = ₹30,00,000 / ₹10,00,000 = 3 times. Dividing profit after tax by interest gives 1.2 and dividing profit before tax by interest gives 2, because both leave out part of the profit available to cover interest.

5.7.5 Interest Coverage Ratio
It is a ratio which deals with the servicing of interest on loan. It is a measure of
security of interest payable on long-term debts. It expresses the relationship
between profits available for payment of interest and the amount of interest
payable. It is calculated as follows:
Interest Coverage Ratio = Net Profit before Interest and Tax
Interest on long-term debts
Significance: It reveals the number of times interest on long-term debts is covered
by the profits available for interest. A higher ratio ensures safety of interest on
debts.
Illustration 11
From the following details, calculate interest coverage

ratio:
Net Profit after tax Rs. 60,000; 15% Long-term debt 10,00,000; and Tax rate
40%.
Solution:
Net Profit after Tax = Rs. 60,000
Tax Rate = 40%
Net Profit before tax = Net profit after tax × 100/(100 – Tax rate)
= Rs. 60,000 × 100/(100 – 40)
= Rs. 1,00,000
Interest on Long-term Debt = 15% of Rs. 10,00,000 = Rs. 1,50,000
Net profit before interest and tax = Net profit before tax + Interest
= Rs. 1,00,000 + Rs. 1,50,000 = Rs. 2,50,000
Interest Coverage Ratio = Net Profit before Interest and
Tax/Interest on long-term debt
= Rs. 2,50,000/Rs. 1,50,000
= 1.67 times.

Interest Coverage Ratio = Net Profit before Interest and

supporting_spans.quote: 6.1 THE BALANCE OF PAYMENTS The balance of payments (BoP) record the transactions in goods, services and assets between residents of a country with the rest of the world for a specified time period typically a year. There are two main accounts in the BoP — the current account and the capital account1. 6.1.1 Current Account Current Account is the record of trade in goods and services and transfer payments. Figure 6.1 illustrates the components of Current Account. Trade in goods includes exports and imports of goods. Trade in services includes factor income and non-factor income transactions. Transfer payments are the receipts which the

of imports of invisibles of a country in a given period of time. Invisibles include services, transfers and flows of income that take place between different countries. Services trade includes both factor and non-factor income. Factor income includes net international earnings on factors of production (like labour, land and capital). Non-factor income is net sale of service products like shipping, banking, tourism, software services, etc. 6.1.2 Capital Account Capital Account records all international transactions of assets. An asset is any one of the forms in which wealth can be held, for example: money, stocks, bonds, Government debt, etc.

Purchase of assets is a debit item on the capital account. If an Indian buys a UK Car Company, it enters capital account transactions as a debit item (as foreign exchange is flowing out of India). On the other hand, sale of assets like sale of share of an Indian company to a Chinese customer is a credit item on the capital account. Fig. 6.2 classifies the items which are a part of capital account transactions. These items are Foreign Direct Investments (FDIs), Foreign Institutional Investments (FIIs), external borrowings and assistance.
